lines.text: arrangements which were familiar to His contemporaries
and hearers. The new and surprising thing is rather the con-
clusion: "So you also ..." The novelty lies in Jesus' sugges-
tion that the relation between God and man is the same as
that between a master and his slave. This was a strange idea
even for the Jewish audience of Jesus. Of course they were
accustomed to speak of God as the almighty all-commanding
Lord, who owes account to no man, but they regarded man
as not being simply God's slave, but rather God's servant,
rewarded by God and entitled to such a reward, and
acquiring merit by the faithful fulfilment of his obligations.
Hence according to Jesus this was false. The suggestion is
not only strange and surprising, but offensive and vexaticus!
Still more is the suggestion offensive to the mind of modern
man; and in this connexion I am thinking not only of the
people of to-day but of man as his being and mode of
thinking has developed during the past few centuries since
the time of the Renaissance. He is of the opinion that in
contrast with earlier and cruder epochs he cherishes a
purified and spiritual idea of God: he thinks that God is not
an arbitrary despot, a master in command of slaves, but as
man himself is conscious of his own moral freedom and
dignity, God too is for him the embodiment of ethical lofty
ideals, a God who is honoured precisely by the fact that man
in the dignity of his freedom can proudly raise his head to
God. God is not sheer power, overwhelming, coercive,
shattering, but rather spiritual power exercising sway over
man through the inner life of the spirit, not humbling man
but rather exalting him. Man would feel it to be demeaning
to recognize himself as the slave of an arbitrary God, whose
action cannot in any way be called to account.
To be sure, while man realizes that he may not call God
to account at the bar of his petty personal desires and needs,
he yet expects that the action of God should evince its
rightness by the criterion of the highest human ideals of
righteousness and goodness! In this way man does call God
to account. And if the process of events in the world and in
